content: 1. If ethambutol-induced toxicity is diagnosed, the drug should be immediately removed from the treatment regimen. 2. Section 4.9 provides a detailed overview of common adverse events associated with tuberculosis (TB) medications and their management strategies. 3. Dermatological reactions such as maculopapular rash and pruritus, which range from mild to severe, are common with drugs like rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. These can be managed with antihistamines, hydrocortisone cream, or low-dose prednisone if other measures fail. Discontinuation of the medication is necessary if systemic symptoms, fever, urticaria, mucous membrane involvement, blistering, lip or eye swelling, wheezing, or airway compromise occur. 4. Transient flushing reactions, which are mild and rare, may occur with rifampicin or pyrazinamide and can be managed with antihistamines. 5. Photosensitivity, a common adverse event with pyrazinamide, can range from mild to severe and should be managed with sunscreen and protective clothing. 6. Severe urticaria or anaphylaxis, though rare, may occur with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, or ethambutol. These require referral for evaluation of potential re-challenge or desensitization in a controlled environment equipped for resuscitation. 7. Rifampicin can cause hypersensitivity reactions, including flu-like syndrome, which is rare with daily dosing but more common with intermittent dosing. Severe hypersensitivity reactions may necessitate discontinuation of rifampicin. 8. Hematological effects, such as marrow suppression leading to decreased hemoglobin, platelets, and white blood cells, are rare but can occur with isoniazid or rifampicin. Severe anemia, leukopenia, or thrombocytopenia may require discontinuation of the drug. 9. Peripheral neuropathy, a common neurotoxic effect of isoniazid in malnourished children or those living with HIV, should be managed by correcting electrolyte abnormalities, evaluating other contributing medications, and adjusting pyridoxine (vitamin B6) doses. Symptoms generally improve after discontinuation of isoniazid. 10. Ophthalmic toxicity, such as optic neuropathy or neuritis, is very rare in children but may occur with ethambutol or isoniazid. Baseline and periodic visual assessments are recommended, and referral is necessary if visual acuity or color discrimination decreases. 11. Hepatitis, ranging from mild to severe, is rare in most children but more common in those living with HIV. Symptoms such as unexplained nausea, decreased appetite, and vomiting may precede jaundice. Discontinuation of the drug is required if liver enzyme levels exceed five times the upper limit of normal or three times with symptoms of hepatitis. 12. Children and adolescents with TB, along with their caregivers, should receive education on the disease and the importance of completing treatment. Support from family members is crucial for successful treatment, especially in younger children. 13. Shorter four-month treatment regimens may improve adherence by reducing the number of required healthcare visits. Child-friendly fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) should be used to simplify administration and adherence. 14. Monitoring of children on TB treatment should occur at specific intervals, including two and four weeks after treatment initiation, at the end of the intensive phase, and every two months until treatment completion. 15. Weight should be measured regularly to adjust dosages as needed, and adherence should be assessed through treatment cards and discussions with caregivers. 16. Follow-up sputum samples may be collected at two months and at treatment completion for children with bacteriological confirmation at diagnosis. However, symptomatic improvement and weight gain are more reliable markers of treatment success. 17. Scheduled clinical monitoring is not required after successful completion of a six-month treatment course, but caregivers should be advised to return if TB symptoms recur. 18. Treatment interruptions should be managed based on the duration and timing of the interruption, as well as the bacteriological status of the patient. For interruptions of less than 14 days, treatment can be continued. For longer interruptions, restarting the intensive phase may be necessary. 19. Treatment failure is defined as the need to terminate or change the treatment regimen due to lack of clinical or bacteriological response, adverse drug reactions, or evidence of drug resistance. Poor adherence is a common cause of treatment failure. 20. Children requiring retreatment for TB should undergo drug susceptibility testing to guide the choice of regimen. If rifampicin resistance is detected, an MDR/RR-TB regimen should be prescribed. 21. Children with previous treatment for unconfirmed TB should not be retreated without referral to a center with expertise in pediatric TB management. 22. All children initiated on TB treatment should be registered, and their progress should be documented to ensure proper management and follow-up.
